theory.title: DDoS: When the Flood Blocks the Path
theory.recap: Anycast distributes traffic to many edge nodes by advertising the same IP from multiple locations. Packet loss occurs when links or servers are overwhelmed. Rate limiters protect servers by dropping excess requests. A DDoS attack weaponizes all of these - flooding a server until it cannot serve legitimate traffic.
theory.plainObjective: The direct path to the server is rate-limited and overwhelmed by the DDoS flood. Find the anycast path to reach a clean edge node that is not overwhelmed.
theory.summary: DDoS mitigation at scale relies on anycast: by advertising the same IP from hundreds of PoPs, the attacker's traffic is spread thin across all of them. No single node is overwhelmed. Cloudflare, Akamai, and AWS Shield all use this architecture to absorb terabits of attack traffic.

bodyParagraphs.heading: What is a DDoS?
bodyParagraphs.text: A DDoS attack floods a server with more traffic than it can handle. Traffic comes from thousands of compromised machines (a botnet). The goal is to exhaust bandwidth, CPU, or connections until legitimate users can't get through.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Rate limiting
bodyParagraphs.text: A rate limiter drops requests above a threshold. Rate limiting protects against simple floods but not distributed attacks - when 10,000 bots each send 10 req/s, the combined flood overwhelms most rate limits.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Anycast as DDoS mitigation
bodyParagraphs.text: The anycast defense: advertise the target IP from hundreds of locations. Instead of all attack traffic hitting one server, it spreads globally. Each node absorbs a fraction. Legitimate users still reach their nearest node.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Clean-pipe routing
bodyParagraphs.text: Traffic is scrubbed at the edge before reaching the origin. DDoS mitigation appliances filter attack signatures; the origin only sees clean traffic. This is what services like Cloudflare and AWS Shield provide.

theory.mission:
Your packet needs to reach the server (10.70.2.10) during an active DDoS attack.

The direct path runs through a rate-limited node overwhelmed by the flood (your requestCount: 5000 exceeds its 100 req/s threshold). Route through the anycast edge node instead - it handles the distributed load and has no rate limit on clean traffic.

termIntroductions.headline: DDoS Attack
termIntroductions.body: A Distributed Denial of Service attack floods a server using thousands of bots. Your packet is a legitimate user caught in the flood: requestCount 5000 represents the combined attack traffic your source appears to be part of. The overwhelmed rate limiter can't distinguish you from the bots.

termIntroductions.headline: Rate Limit Exceeded
termIntroductions.body: The direct server's rate limiter threshold is 100 req/s. During the DDoS flood (5000 req/s from your network's IP range), the limiter blocks all traffic from your source - legitimate or not. The anycast edge absorbs the distributed load differently. Find the clean path.

termIntroductions.headline: Anycast Absorption
termIntroductions.body: The anycast edge distributes DDoS traffic across hundreds of PoPs globally. Your traffic arrives at the nearest clean edge - the flood is diluted because attackers worldwide are routed to different nodes. This edge isn't overwhelmed, so your packet passes through to the clean-pipe destination.
